topics.title: How People Kept Food From Rotting Before the Fridge
topics.safe_title: How People Kept Food From Rotting Before the Fridge
topics.angle: It is August, there is no fridge, and your family has to eat in February. Open with a life-or-death kitchen problem, then a ladder of real solutions, each with a mini-story, how it physically works (what bacteria need and what each method takes away from them: water, warmth, air) and a way to picture it. Root cellars and why the ground stays cool. Salt and the salt cod fleets. Smoke houses. Drying: Andean chuno, potatoes freeze-dried by mountain nights, and pemmican on the plains. Sugar and honey, why honey does not spoil. Fermentation: sauerkraut on James Cook's ships against scurvy, and kimchi in buried clay pots. Frederic Tudor of Boston, laughed at for shipping ice to Martinique in 1806, later to Calcutta in 1833, and sawdust as insulation. Nicolas Appert sealing food in glass jars for a French prize in 1809, Peter Durand's tin can in 1810, and the can opener that arrived decades later. Mohammed Bah Abba's clay pot-in-pot cooler in northern Nigeria in the 1990s. End with Clarence Birdseye learning fast freezing from Inuit fishers in Labrador around 1912 to 1915. Do not repeat the Persian ice house from our winter video. Halal: no pork, ham, bacon or lard, salted and smoked meat is beef, mutton or fish; no wine, beer or spirits at all, and no alcohol as a preservative.

topics.title: How Long Would You Survive in Every Era of History?
topics.safe_title: How Long Would You Survive in Every Era of History?
topics.angle: Drop the viewer, a modern person with no special skills, into Ice Age Europe, Bronze Age Egypt, Imperial Rome, a Viking-age farm, medieval London in 1348, a sailing ship of 1750, an 1850s factory town. Each era a full mini-story: first 24 hours, what kills you first (cold, water, infection, hunger, law), what would save you, a survival estimate in days. Real data: Roman life expectancy, medieval child mortality, Black Death deaths share, scurvy on ships (Lind 1747), London cholera 1854 (John Snow). Ladder structure, each era harder or weirder in a surprising way; end: the safest era twist. Ask the viewer to keep score.
topics.hedge: Survival numbers are informed estimates, not data.

topics.title: How People Survived Winter Before Electricity
topics.safe_title: How People Survived Winter Before Electricity
topics.angle: Six real systems, each with the physics opened so the viewer could rebuild it: the Inuit igloo (raised sleeping platform, cold trap entrance, snow as insulator, seal-oil lamp); the Roman hypocaust; the Korean ondol floor; the Russian masonry stove people slept on; the medieval box bed and shared hall with animals as heat; the Persian yakhchal that stored ice through the desert summer as a twist finale. Real temperatures and materials. Human scenes: a family in a blizzard. End: what we forgot, thermal mass and insulating the person not the room, and why a modern house fails in a power cut.
topics.hedge: Exact indoor temperatures vary between reports.

topics.title: How People Survived Summer Heat Before Air Conditioning
topics.safe_title: How People Stayed Cool Before Air Conditioning
topics.angle: July, 46 C, no electricity, and a family has to sleep tonight. Ladder of real solutions, each with how it physically works: thick mud and adobe walls that delay the heat by hours (thermal mass), the badgir windcatchers of Yazd in Iran, the qanat underground channels that cool the air that passes over water, the yakhchal is NOT repeated (it was in our winter video, only mention once), the mashrabiya wooden screens of Cairo and the courtyard house, wet reed mats over doors in ancient Egypt (evaporative cooling), sleeping on the roof under the stars, the siesta and the timing of the day, the clay water jar that sweats to stay cool. Then the 1902 twist: Willis Carrier invented air conditioning for a printing plant in Brooklyn, not for people. End: what modern architects are copying back from the past. Halal: no pork or alcohol, no idols or pagan rituals shown as truth; women in long loose clothing with headscarves; dot eyes.

topics.title: How People Cleaned Their Teeth Before Toothpaste
topics.safe_title: How People Cleaned Their Teeth Before Toothpaste
topics.angle: A toothache in 1700 with no dentist in the town. Ladder: chewing sticks and the miswak (Salvadora persica) used across Arabia and Africa for centuries, with modern studies on its natural fluoride and antibacterial effect (WHO mentions chewing sticks); Egyptian tooth powder recipes; the bristle toothbrush in China around 1498; William Addis making a toothbrush in an English prison around 1780; Pierre Fauchard, the father of modern dentistry, 1728; the tooth-key and why tooth pulling was a street job; the first toothpaste in a tube in 1890s; fluoride in the 20th century. Honest catch: much ancient tooth care did not work and hurt, some powders wore away the enamel. End: why our ancestors' teeth were sometimes healthier (less sugar). topics.title: How People Found Their Way Before Maps and GPS
topics.angle: A ship in the open ocean at night, no land in sight for weeks. Ladder: the Polynesian wayfinders reading swells and stars (Hokule'a voyage 1976), the Pole Star and latitude, the Arab and Indian Ocean navigators and Ahmad ibn Majid's 15th century guide, the kamal (a wooden card on a knotted string to measure the star's height), the magnetic compass from China, the astrolabe, the longitude problem and John Harrison's sea clock (1761), desert caravans reading dunes and stars. Honest catch: thousands of ships were still lost. End: what happens in our brain when we use GPS (Maguire's London taxi drivers study 2000). topics.title: How People Got Clean Water Before Pipes
topics.safe_title: How People Got Clean Water Before Taps
topics.angle: A village in a dry summer, the river is brown and people are getting sick. Ladder: hand-dug wells and why depth matters, the qanats of Persia, the stepwells of India (Chand Baori), Roman aqueducts and the 1-in-4800 slope, the Basilica Cistern of Istanbul (6th century), sand and charcoal filters, boiling, copper vessels, rainwater on rooftops, the water carriers of old cities. Twist: John Snow and the Broad Street pump in London 1854, the first time someone proved water carried disease. End: two billion people still lack safe water today (WHO), and the old tricks that still save lives. topics.title: How People Knew the Time Before Clocks
topics.safe_title: How People Told Time Before Clocks
topics.angle: A town at dawn with no clock anywhere, and yet everyone meets on time. Ladder: the shadow of a stick and sundials, Egyptian water clocks (clepsydra), candle clocks with marks, sand glasses on ships, Al-Jazari's elephant water clock (1206), the call to prayer that divided the day for whole cities, ship watches and bells, the Chinese incense clock, then Huygens' pendulum clock 1656 and how railways created time zones in 1883. Twist: noon was different in every town until the trains. End: what we lost when time became exact. Halal: no pork or alcohol, no idols or pagan rituals shown as truth; women in long loose clothing with headscarves; dot eyes.
